expectedText:
DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE REMEDY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE REMEDY INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's ex parte civil seizure remedy, 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2), a distinct procedural mechanism separate from the ordinary injunction, damages, and attorney's-fee remedies available under 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(3). It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning Acme, Inc.'s trade secret, described as follows: Acme's proprietary customer-pricing algorithm and associated source code, in a situation involving Beta Corp. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what the statute says about when a court may order the seizure of property to prevent a trade secret's propagation or dissemination, what an applicant must show, what protections the statute builds in for the party whose property is seized and for third parties, and what liability can follow a wrongful or excessive seizure. It does not itself determine whether a seizure order would be sought, granted, denied, dissolved, or modified in any specific case, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and is meant as a companion to, this project's existing Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheet (which addresses the ordinary injunction remedy under section 1836(b)(3)(A)) and its existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document (whose federal-remedies clause identifies the civil seizure provision by name but does not quote or describe it) -- this Information Sheet is what fills that specific, previously-disclosed gap.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: AN EXTRAORDINARY, EX PARTE REMEDY
The Defend Trade Secrets Act authorizes a court, based on an affidavit or verified complaint meeting the statute's requirements, to issue an order for the seizure of property necessary to prevent the propagation or dissemination of the trade secret at issue in the action. The statute frames this as an extraordinary remedy available only on ex parte application -- meaning the application may be made and the order may be sought without prior notice to the party whose property would be seized -- and the statute itself limits the remedy to "extraordinary circumstances," a threshold distinct from the showing required for an ordinary injunction under the same section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Based on an affidavit or verified complaint satisfying the requirements of this paragraph, the court may, upon ex parte application but only in extraordinary circumstances, issue an order providing for the seizure of property necessary to prevent the propagation or dissemination of the trade secret that is the subject of the action."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- application (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of what 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(A)(i) authorizes on its face -- not a claim about how often courts actually grant this relief, which circumstances courts have treated as sufficiently "extraordinary," or whether any specific set of facts would qualify. Courts have applied this remedy sparingly since its 2016 enactment, and the specific findings a court must make before granting it are addressed in this document's companion clauses rather than in this one. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota already exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law on how courts have applied this ex parte, extraordinary-circumstances threshold is included here; only the statutory text is quoted.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: REQUIRED FINDINGS ON NECESSITY AND HARM
Before granting a seizure application, the statute requires the court to find that it clearly appears from specific facts that an order under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65 (the ordinary preliminary-injunction rule) or another form of equitable relief would be inadequate because the party to be ordered would evade, avoid, or otherwise not comply with it; that immediate and irreparable injury will occur without the seizure; and that the harm to the applicant of denying the application outweighs the harm to the legitimate interests of the person against whom seizure would be ordered, and substantially outweighs the harm to any third parties who may be harmed by the seizure. The statute also requires findings that the person against whom seizure would be ordered would destroy, move, hide, or otherwise make the property inaccessible to the court if given notice, and that the applicant has not publicized the requested seizure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "an order issued pursuant to Rule 65 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure or another form of equitable relief would be inadequate to achieve the purpose of this paragraph because the party to which the order would be issued would evade, avoid, or otherwise not comply with such an order"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii)(I)-(III) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- requirements for issuing order (inadequacy of other relief, irreparable injury, balance of harms); subclauses of the same paragraph as the citation in the companion clause on merits findings, not an independent source of it (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the necessity- and harm-related findings 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii) requires before a seizure order may issue -- not a claim about how any court would weigh these factors on particular facts. This clause paraphrases and summarizes five of the statute's eight numbered findings (subclauses (I), (II), (III), (VII), and (VIII)); the remaining three findings, concerning the merits of the trade secret and misappropriation claims and the location of the property, are quoted in a companion clause of this document rather than repeated here. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was not separately attempted beyond the single rate-limited search already disclosed elsewhere in this document; that search returned an HTTP 429 error before any results were retrieved, so no case law interpreting these findings is included here.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: REQUIRED FINDINGS ON THE MERITS AND LOCATION OF PROPERTY
In addition to the necessity and harm findings, the statute requires the court to find that the applicant is likely to succeed in showing that the information is a trade secret and that the person against whom seizure would be ordered either misappropriated the trade secret by improper means or conspired to use improper means to misappropriate it. The court must also find that the person against whom seizure would be ordered has actual possession of both the trade secret and the property to be seized, and that the application describes with reasonable particularity the matter to be seized and, to the extent reasonable, identifies the location where it is to be seized.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the applicant is likely to succeed in showing that— (aa) the information is a trade secret ; and (bb) the person against whom seizure would be ordered— (AA) misappropriated the trade secret of the applicant by improper means ; or (BB) conspired to use improper means to misappropriate the trade secret of the applicant"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii)(IV)-(VI) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- requirements for issuing order (likelihood of success, possession, particularity); subclauses of the same paragraph as the citation in the companion clause on necessity/harm findings, not an independent source of it (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the merits- and location-related findings 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii) requires -- not a claim that any particular information qualifies as a trade secret or that any particular conduct constitutes misappropriation by improper means on the facts described elsewhere in this document. This clause quotes and paraphrases three of the statute's eight numbered findings (subclauses (IV), (V), and (VI)); the other five, concerning necessity and harm, are addressed in a companion clause rather than repeated here, and both clauses draw from the same statutory subparagraph rather than independent sources. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt already disclosed in this document's other clauses.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: NARROWEST SEIZURE AND PROTECTION OF SEIZED PROPERTY
If a seizure order issues, the statute requires it to provide for the narrowest seizure of property necessary to achieve the statute's purpose, and to direct that the seizure be conducted in a manner that minimizes any interruption of third parties' business operations and, to the extent possible, does not interrupt the legitimate business operations of the person accused of misappropriation. The order must also be accompanied by a provision protecting the seized property from disclosure -- prohibiting access by the applicant or the person against whom the order is directed, and prohibiting copies of the seized property -- until the parties have an opportunity to be heard at the seizure hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "provide for the narrowest seizure of property necessary to achieve the purpose of this paragraph and direct that the seizure be conducted in a manner that minimizes any interruption of the business operations of third parties and, to the extent possible, does not interrupt the legitimate business operations of the person accused of misappropriating the trade secret"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(B)(ii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- elements of order (narrowest seizure); part of the same subparagraph as the companion clause on the hearing deadline and security bond, not an independent source of it (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of what 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(B) requires an issued seizure order to contain -- not a claim about how narrowly any particular court has construed "narrowest seizure of property necessary" on specific facts. This clause quotes and paraphrases two of the six elements a seizure order must include under subparagraph (B) (clauses (ii) and (iii)(I)); the hearing-deadline and security-bond elements of the same subparagraph are addressed in a companion clause rather than repeated here. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: SEVEN-DAY HEARING DEADLINE AND SECURITY BOND
A seizure order must set a date for a hearing at the earliest possible time, and not later than seven days after the order issues, unless the party against whom the order is directed and others harmed by it consent to a later date; any party against whom the order issued, or any person harmed by it, may move at any time to dissolve or modify the order after giving notice to the applicant. The order must also require the person who obtained it to post security, in an amount the court determines adequate, for the payment of damages that any person may be entitled to recover from a wrongful or excessive seizure or attempted seizure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "set a date for a hearing described in subparagraph (F) at the earliest possible time, and not later than 7 days after the order has issued, unless the party against whom the order is directed and others harmed by the order consent to another date for the hearing"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(B)(v) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- elements of order (hearing deadline); part of the same subparagraph as the companion clause on narrowness and disclosure protection, not an independent source of it (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the hearing-timing and security-bond requirements 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(B) imposes on an issued seizure order -- not a claim about what amount of security any court would set, or how quickly any specific hearing would actually be scheduled. This clause quotes and paraphrases two of the six required elements of a seizure order under subparagraph (B) (clauses (v) and (vi)); the narrowest-seizure and disclosure-protection elements of the same subparagraph are addressed in a companion clause rather than repeated here. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: EXECUTION ONLY BY LAW ENFORCEMENT, NOT THE APPLICANT
The statute requires that service of the seizure order be made by a federal law enforcement officer, who then carries out the seizure. The court may allow state or local law enforcement to participate, but may not permit the applicant or any agent of the applicant to participate in the seizure itself. At the request of law enforcement, the court may allow an unaffiliated technical expert bound by a court-approved non-disclosure agreement to participate if doing so would aid an efficient, minimally burdensome execution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The court shall order that service of a copy of the order under this paragraph, and the submissions of the applicant to obtain the order, shall be made by a Federal law enforcement officer who, upon making service, shall carry out the seizure under the order. The court may allow State or local law enforcement officials to participate, but may not permit the applicant or any agent of the applicant to participate in the seizure."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(E) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- service of order (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of who the statute requires to execute a seizure order under 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(E) -- not a claim about how this requirement operates in practice in any particular judicial district or how any specific seizure would actually be staffed. This clause quotes and paraphrases subparagraph (E) in full; it does not address the separate custody-of-materials provisions of subparagraph (D), which are covered in a companion clause. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: CUSTODY OF THE COURT AND CONFIDENTIALITY PROTECTIONS
Materials seized under the statute are taken into the custody of the court, which must secure them from physical and electronic access during the seizure and while in its custody. If the seized material includes or is stored on a storage medium, the court must prohibit that medium from being connected to a network or the internet without both parties' consent, until the required seizure hearing. The court must also take appropriate measures to protect the confidentiality of seized materials unrelated to the trade secret information ordered seized, unless the person against whom the order was entered consents to disclosure, and the court may appoint a special master -- bound by a court-approved non-disclosure agreement -- to locate and isolate the misappropriated trade secret information and facilitate return of unrelated property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Any materials seized under this paragraph shall be taken into the custody of the court. The court shall secure the seized material from physical and electronic access during the seizure and while in the custody of the court."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(D)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- materials in custody of court (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the custody and confidentiality safeguards 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(D) imposes once property has been seized -- not a claim about how any specific court's clerk's office or IT security practices would actually implement these safeguards, or about whether a special master would be appointed in any particular case. This clause summarizes and quotes from subparagraph (D)'s four clauses together; it does not separately address the publicity-protection provisions of subparagraph (C), which are distinct language in the same paragraph. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

DTSA CIVIL SEIZURE: LIABILITY FOR A WRONGFUL OR EXCESSIVE SEIZURE
A person who suffers damage because of a wrongful or excessive seizure has a cause of action against the applicant who obtained the seizure order, and is entitled to the same relief provided under the parallel wrongful-seizure provision of the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. section 1116(d)(11) (a trademark-counterfeiting seizure statute the DTSA's drafters used as a model). The statute specifies that the security the applicant was required to post does not limit third parties' recovery of damages. Separately, at any time -- including on an ex parte motion -- a party or a person claiming an interest in the seized material may move to have material stored on a storage medium encrypted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A person who suffers damage by reason of a wrongful or excessive seizure under this paragraph has a cause of action against the applicant for the order under which such seizure was made, and shall be entitled to the same relief as is provided under section 34(d)(11) of the Trademark Act of 1946 ( 15 U.S.C. 1116(d)(11) )."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(G) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- action for damage caused by wrongful seizure (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1836)
  Known gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the wrongful-seizure cause of action and encryption-motion mechanism in 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(G) and (H) -- not a claim about the amount of damages any court has awarded, or how the incorporated Lanham Act relief standard, 15 U.S.C. section 1116(d)(11), has actually been applied in a DTSA seizure case (that provision's own text is not independently fetched or quoted in this clause; it is identified here only as a cross-reference within the DTSA text quoted). No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document, so no case applying the wrongful-seizure cause of action is included here.

expectedJSON.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the wrongful-seizure cause of action and encryption-motion mechanism in 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(G) and (H) -- not a claim about the amount of damages any court has awarded, or how the incorporated Lanham Act relief standard, 15 U.S.C. section 1116(d)(11), has actually been applied in a DTSA seizure case (that provision's own text is not independently fetched or quoted in this clause; it is identified here only as a cross-reference within the DTSA text quoted). No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document, so no case applying the wrongful-seizure cause of action is included here.
